2.text: After catching a soul, they chop it to pieces, cook it in a kettle, and

3.text: feed their children with it.¹ A shaman said to me, —

4.text: “We are surrounded by enemies. ‘Spirits’ always walk about invisibly with gaping mouths.

5.text: We are always cringing, and distributing gifts on all sides, asking protection of one, giving ransom

6.text: to another, and unable to obtain anything whatsoever gratuitously.”

7.text: Aiñanwaˊt,² in his curious description of the “bad years of small-pox” on

8.text: the western tundra of the Kolyma, says as follows: —

9.text: “Then I had a dream. A cloud came from above, like darkness. It approached slowly, like

10.text: a thick fog. I saw it approaching, and all grew dark around me. It was a black crowd, a gathering

11.text: of men clad in black. In the bright mid-day they darkened the sun completely. I asked those

12.text: nearest, ‘What are you coming for?’ They answered, ‘We came to devour you!’ — ‘Oh,’ I said,

13.text: ‘let me help you at first.’ I picked up from the ground a piece of wood, and suddenly I saw

14.text: myself soaring upwards. Then I began moving to and fro, and struck with the stick upon the top

15.text: of all tents of my camp. I struck down all the tents, but these were in reality the souls of my

16.text: wife and children whom I struck down. Thus I killed all of mine with my own hand. And from

17.text: the time of that dream the disease could seize all of my family.”³

18.text: “Spirits” like the inner organs of the human body, — the heart, the

19.text: kidneys, and especially the liver. “Keˊlᴇ is fond of liver” (Keˊlᴇ pontaˊɪrɪnkên),

20.text: says a proverb. The following tale is given as the reason for their peculiar

22.text: “Once upon a time an old woman keˊlᴇ lived with her little son near a village of men. She

23.text: had nothing to eat, and every time the villagers happened to kill a seal or a walrus, she asked for

24.text: its liver, and she and her child lived on that. At last the villagers got weary of the tribute.

25.text: They enticed her son to accompany them for a drive across the ice, and killed him. Then,

26.text: bringing back his liver, they gave it to the keˊlᴇ-woman. She did not recognize it, and, taking it

27.text: home, roasted a portion over her lamp. The remaining portion she laid down near by. Suddenly

28.text: it turned into live lice, which crawled away in all directions. After that, the keˊlet, in revenge,

29.text: began to seek for human liver.”

30.text: The same taste for liver is ascribed by the Koryak to their kaˊla.⁴

31.text: The keˊlet are not exempt from the attacks of shamans, who can deal

32.text: with them in the same way as they deal with men. The keˊlet, on their

33.text: part, call shamans keˊlet. If a “spirit” drives with a reindeer-team and a

34.text: shaman steps on the rear part of the runners of his sledge, the team will

35.text: immediately stop, because the reindeer are aware of the presence of the

36.text: shaman. The “spirits,” unable to understand what has happened, will seek

37.text: for some natural cause. The same thing happens to men whose sledges may

38.text: be stopped by “spirits.” I collected numerous stories about “spirits” attacking

39.text: human villages, and about shamans retaliating in exactly the same way.
